summary.text: The Poincaré series in question is defined to be the displayed rational formal power series itself, so the claimed equality follows immediately from that definition. No independent argument about Siegel theta series or odd unimodular lattices is used.

full_proof.text:
Work in the ring \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\) of formal power series with rational coefficients, and let \(X\) denote the formal series \(x\). Put
\[
N(X)=1+X^{18}
\]
and
\[
D(X)=(1-X)(1-X^8)(1-X^{12})(1-X^{24}).
\]
Each factor of \(D\) has constant coefficient \(1\), so \(D\) itself has constant coefficient \(1\). A formal power series over a field is invertible precisely when its constant coefficient is nonzero. Thus \(D^{-1}\) exists in \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\), and the series
\[
G(X):=N(X)D(X)^{-1}
 =\frac{1+X^{18}}{(1-X)(1-X^8)(1-X^{12})(1-X^{24})}
\]
is well-defined.

For completeness, this series has the claimed coefficient interpretation. In the formal power-series ring, the geometric-series identity gives
\[
\frac1{1-X^d}=\sum_{j\ge 0}X^{dj}
\]
for every positive integer \(d\). Consequently,
\[
\frac1{D(X)}
 =\left(\sum_{b_1\ge0}X^{b_1}\right)
  \left(\sum_{b_8\ge0}X^{8b_8}\right)
  \left(\sum_{b_{12}\ge0}X^{12b_{12}}\right)
  \left(\sum_{b_{24}\ge0}X^{24b_{24}}\right).
\]
The coefficient of \(X^m\) in this product is therefore the number
\[
f(m)=\#\left\{(b_1,b_8,b_{12},b_{24})\in\mathbb N^4:
 b_1+8b_8+12b_{12}+24b_{24}=m\right\}.
\]
This count is finite. One may compute it by first choosing
\(b_{24}=\ell\), where
\(0\le \ell\le\lfloor m/24\rfloor\), then choosing
\(b_{12}=k\), where
\[
0\le k\le\left\lfloor\frac{m-24\ell}{12}\right\rfloor,
\]
and finally choosing
\[
0\le b_8\le
\left\lfloor\frac{m-24\ell-12k}{8}\right\rfloor.
\]
Once these three choices have been made, \(b_1\) is uniquely forced to be
\[
b_1=m-24\ell-12k-8b_8,
\]
which is nonnegative by the bound on \(b_8\). Thus this enumeration is exactly the nested finite sum used in the definition of \(f(m)\).

Multiplication by \(1+X^{18}\) gives
\[
G(X)=\sum_{m\ge0}f(m)X^m+X^{18}\sum_{m\ge0}f(m)X^m.
\]
Hence the coefficient of \(X^n\) is
\[
a(n)=
\begin{cases}
f(n),&n<18,\\
f(n)+f(n-18),&n\ge18.
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, it is \(f(n)+f(n-18)\) when \(18\le n\), and \(f(n)\) otherwise. This explains the displayed generating function and the numerical sequence A097913.

It remains to prove the theorem as it is stated. In that statement, the expression called
“the Poincaré series for genus-2 Siegel theta series of odd unimodular lattices” is not specified by an independent construction from lattices, theta series, graded vector spaces, or dimensions. Instead, that named series is defined by
\[
P_{\mathrm{genus},\mathrm{odd}}(X):=G(X).
\]
Therefore, after expanding this definition, the desired assertion
\[
G(X)=P_{\mathrm{genus},\mathrm{odd}}(X)
\]
becomes simply
\[
G(X)=G(X),
\]
which follows from reflexivity of equality. There are no reductions or case splits beyond the coefficient discussion above; the theorem itself is a direct consequence of the definition of its right-hand side.

Thus the stated equality is proved. It is important to delimit exactly what this argument establishes: because the right-hand side was defined to equal the rational generating series, the argument does not prove that an independently defined graded space of genus-2 Siegel theta series of odd unimodular lattices has these dimensions. Such a substantive version of the conjecture would require an independent definition of that graded space or its Poincaré series and an invariant-theoretic argument identifying its Hilbert–Poincaré series with \(G(X)\). No such independent object or assertion is present in the stated theorem.
